3.text: from one source or another; but after a couple of days the time arrives when

4.text: all the guests and the casual comers must leave the camp, and a friendless

5.text: family often does not know where to go. For instance, the man called

6.text: Scratching-Woman, whose name has been mentioned before, told me the

7.text: following about his own infancy. His father was a weak and shiftless little

8.text: fellow, who had but few reindeer, and even those he lost one winter in a big

9.text: snow-storm. This happened near the Russian village Markova, on the Anadyr

10.text: River. Then the parents of Scratching-Woman came to Markova afoot, drag-

11.text: ging behind them a sledge, on which lay their only son and their scanty

12.text: belongings. They staid in Markova about two months, and could get but

13.text: very little to eat; so that at the end of that time the father died, mainly

14.text: from hunger, and the mother and son nearly followed his example. Some

15.text: Reindeer Chukchee, who came to Markova for trading-purposes, however,

16.text: took them back to the Chukchee camps; and from that time on they scarcely

17.text: had any place in which to live. Nobody wanted them in his camp; and if

18.text: they staid too long, nobody cared whether they had anything to eat or not.

19.text: Thus they lived in constant hunger. They did not have even a single driving-

20.text: reindeer, and were obliged to wander from place to place on foot. When

21.text: the boy grew older, he endeavored to get something from his richer neigh-

22.text: bors by performing various small services. He carried large bundles of fuel,

24.text: a piece of putrid meat, or a reindeer-paunch filled with rancid blood. “My

25.text: growth was stunted by that hunger,” said Scratching-Woman, “and that is
